All rings below are commutative with identity, and an integral domain is required to satisfy \(1\ne0\). For each integral domain \(D\), let \(K=\operatorname{Frac}(D)\) be its field of fractions, let \(X\) be one indeterminate over \(K\), and define the ring of integer-valued polynomials by
\[
\operatorname{Int}(D)=\{f\in K[X]:f(a)\in D\text{ for every }a\in D\}.
\]
For any ring \(A\), its Krull dimension \(\dim A\) is the supremum of the lengths \(r\) of strict chains of prime ideals \(\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\mathfrak p_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_r\).

Determine explicitly the complete set
\[
\mathcal S=\bigl\{(\dim D[X],\dim\operatorname{Int}(D)):\ D\text{ is an integral domain and both displayed dimensions are finite}\bigr\}
\]
as a subset of \(\mathbb Z_{>0}^{\,2}\), where \(\mathbb Z_{>0}\) denotes the positive integers.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer is an explicit description of the entire subset \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\), giving a necessary-and-sufficient criterion for a pair of positive integers to occur. It must establish both that every included pair is realized by an integral domain and that no excluded pair can occur.

9	In particular, there is **no upper bound** on \(\dim\operatorname{Int}(D)\) in terms of \(\dim D[X]\), even when the latter is \(3\).
10	
11	We prove the restrictions first, then give the realizations. The main construction is included; no realization theorem about integer-valued polynomials is being assumed.
12	
13	## 1. Dimension facts used below
14	
15	We use the following classical facts about polynomial rings, valuation rings, and pullbacks.
16	
17	1. If \(A\) is a finite-dimensional domain and \(Q\in\operatorname{Spec}(A[T])\), with \(p=Q\cap A\), the one-variable special-chain theorem gives
18	   \[
19	   \operatorname{ht}Q\le \operatorname{ht}(p[T])+1.
20	   \]
21	   If \(Q\ne p[T]\), equality holds. Also
22	   \[
23	   \dim A+1\le \dim A[T]\le2\dim A+1.
24	   \]
25	
26	2. A finite-rank valuation domain of rank \(s\) has polynomial-ring dimension \(s+1\).
27	
28	3. If all valuation overrings of \(A\) have rank at most \(s\), every domain between \(A[T]\) and \(\operatorname{Frac}(A)(T)\) has dimension at most \(s+1\). This follows from the valuation characterization of dimension and the valuation transcendence inequality.
29	
30	4. If \(\dim A=1\) and \(\dim A[T]=2\), all valuation overrings of \(A\) have rank at most \(1\).
31	
32	   Here is a standard way to obtain the last fact. Every \(m[T]\), for \(m\) maximal in \(A\), has height \(1\). Thus no upper to zero is contained in \(m[T]\). Consequently \(A\) is quasi-Prüfer. The classical quasi-Prüfer criterion says that its integral closure is Prüfer. Integral extension preserves dimension, so this integral closure is a one-dimensional Prüfer domain. Every valuation overring of \(A\) contains it and therefore has rank at most \(1\).
33	
34	We also repeatedly use the elementary pullback observation:
35	
36	> If \(A\subseteq T\) share an ideal \(I\), their spectra outside \(V(I)\) are naturally isomorphic.
37	
38	Indeed, \(A_i=T_i\) for every \(i\in I\).
39	
40	Here is a useful consequence, with its proof.
41	
42	### Conductor dimension lemma
43	
44	Suppose \(A\subseteq T\) share a nonzero prime ideal \(I\), and put \(C=A/I\). Suppose:
45	- every chain of primes of \(T\) not containing \(I\) has length at most \(1\);
46	- \(\operatorname{ht}_A I=1\).
47	
48	Then
49	\[
50	\dim A=1+\dim C. \tag{1}
51	\]
52	
53	For a chain meeting \(V(I)\), replace the part preceding its first prime in \(V(I)\) by \(0\subset I\), omitting repetitions. The outside-\(V(I)\) part had length at most \(1\), so this does not shorten the chain. This proves the upper bound. Concatenating \(0\subset I\) with chains in \(C\) proves the lower bound.
54	
55	## 2. Restrictions on the pairs
56	
57	Write
58	\[
59	a=\dim D[X],\qquad b=\dim\operatorname{Int}(D).
60	\]
61	
62	### 2.1 Localization away from finite residue fields
63	
64	If \(p\in\operatorname{Spec}D\) and \(D/p\) is infinite, then
65	\[
66	\operatorname{Int}(D)_{D\setminus p}=D_p[X]. \tag{2}
67	\]
68	
69	To prove this, take \(f\in\operatorname{Int}(D)\) of degree at most \(n\). Choose \(a_0,\ldots,a_n\in D\) with distinct images modulo \(p\). The Vandermonde determinant is a unit in \(D_p\); interpolation therefore puts every coefficient of \(f\) in \(D_p\). The reverse inclusion after localization is immediate.
70	
71	For such a \(p\), set
72	\[
73	J_p=\operatorname{Int}(D)\cap pD_p[X].
74	\]
75	By (2),
76	\[
77	\operatorname{ht}J_p=\operatorname{ht}(p[X]).
78	\]
79	Reduction modulo \(p\) identifies \(\operatorname{Int}(D)/J_p\) with a subring of
80	\(\operatorname{Frac}(D/p)[X]\) consisting of polynomials integer-valued on \(D/p\), and containing \((D/p)[X]\). Evaluation at zero is a surjection onto \(D/p\), with nonzero prime kernel. Hence
81	\[
82	b\ge \operatorname{ht}(p[X])+\dim(D/p)+1. \tag{3}
83	\]
84	
85	In particular, evaluation directly gives the familiar bound
86	\[
87	b\ge\dim D+1. \tag{4}
88	\]
89	
90	### 2.2 The general lower bound \(b\ge a-1\)
91	
92	Choose a prime \(Q\) of \(D[X]\) of height \(a\), and put \(m=Q\cap D\).
93	
94	If \(D/m\) is infinite, (2) preserves the entire chain below \(Q\), and \(b\ge a\).
95	
96	Otherwise \(D/m\) is a finite field, so \(m\) is maximal. Since \(Q\) has maximal possible height, it is maximal, and
97	\[
98	a=\operatorname{ht}(m[X])+1.
99	\]
100	Choose a chain of length \(a-1\) ending at \(m[X]\), and let \(P\) be its penultimate prime. Put \(p=P\cap D\). Necessarily \(p\subsetneq m\), so \(D/p\) is infinite. The special-chain inequality gives
101	\[
102	a-2\le\operatorname{ht}P\le\operatorname{ht}(p[X])+1.
103	\]
104	Using (3) and \(\dim(D/p)\ge1\), we obtain
105	\[
106	b\ge\operatorname{ht}(p[X])+2\ge a-1. \tag{5}
107	\]
108	The cases of chains too short to have the indicated penultimate prime follow at once from (4).
109	
110	### 2.3 The two small first coordinates
111	
112	If \(a=1\), then \(D\) is a field. Thus \(\operatorname{Int}(D)=D[X]\), giving \((a,b)=(1,1)\).
113	
114	If \(a=2\), then \(\dim D=1\). Fact 4 above and the valuation transcendence inequality imply \(b\le2\), while (4) gives \(b\ge2\). Thus \((a,b)=(2,2)\).
115	
116	This proves all the asserted restrictions.
117	
118	## 3. A family realizing \((3,b)\) for every \(b\ge2\)
119	
120	We construct, for every integer \(r\ge0\), a domain \(D_r\) satisfying
121	\[
122	\dim D_r=1,\qquad
123	\dim D_r[X]=3,\qquad
124	\dim\operatorname{Int}(D_r)=r+2. \tag{6}
125	\]
126	
127	Throughout, let \(k=\mathbb F_3\).
128	
129	### 3.1 The valuation rings
130	
131	For \(r\ge1\), take
132	\[
133	L=k(u_1,\ldots,u_r),\qquad K=L(t).
134	\]
135	Let \(V_0\) be the \(t\)-adic valuation ring of \(K\), with maximal ideal \(M_0\) and residue field \(L\).
136	
137	Let \(B\) be the rank-\(r\) lexicographic monomial valuation ring of \(L\), with parameters \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\). Its residue field is \(k\). Compose this valuation with the \(t\)-adic valuation to obtain
138	\[
139	W=B+M_0\subset V_0.
140	\]
141	Thus \(W\) has rank \(r+1\), \(M_0\) is its height-one prime, and \(W/M_0=B\).
142	
143	For \(r=0\), instead take
144	\[
145	L=k(u),\qquad K=L(t),\qquad W=V_0,\qquad B=L.
146	\]
147	In both cases \(L/k\) is transcendental, \(\dim B=r\), and \(-1\) is not a square in the residue field of \(W\).
148	
149	We need a sequence of DVRs \(V_i\) of \(K\) with:
150	
151	- finite residue fields \(k_i\) of odd degrees over \(k\), with \(|k_i|\to\infty\);
152	- for every \(x\in K^\times\), the sign of its value at \(V_i\) eventually equals its sign at \(W\). In particular,
153	  \[
154	  x\in W \Longleftrightarrow x\in V_i\text{ for all sufficiently large }i, \tag{7}
155	  \]
156	  and units of \(W\) are eventually units of \(V_i\).
157	
158	Here are explicit instructions establishing their existence. Let
159	\(k_i=\mathbb F_{3^{d_i}}\), where \(d_i\) are strictly increasing odd integers, and choose a generator \(\alpha_i\) of \(k_i/k\).
160	
161	For \(r\ge1\), choose integers \(n_i\to\infty\) and embed \(K\) into \(k_i((z))\) with
162	\[
163	u_r=z,\quad
164	u_j=z^{\,n_i^{r-j}}+\text{higher terms}\quad(j<r),\quad
165	t=\alpha_i z^{\,n_i^r}+\text{higher terms}.
166	\]
167	Choose the series other than \(z\) algebraically independent over \(k_i(z)\). Such choices exist even with any prescribed finite initial segments: the algebraic closure of a countable field is countable, whereas each set of permitted series is uncountable.
168	
169	The induced valuation has value group \(\mathbb Z\), and its residue field is exactly \(k_i\): the residue of \(t/u_r^{n_i^r}\) is \(\alpha_i\).
170	
171	For each fixed polynomial, sufficiently large \(n_i\) makes its distinct monomials have distinct weights, ordered lexicographically. This proves the required eventual sign agreement.
172	
173	For \(r=0\), use
174	\[
175	t=z,\qquad u=\alpha_i+\text{higher terms},
176	\]
177	with \(u\) transcendental over \(k_i(z)\). Since the degrees of \(\alpha_i\) tend to infinity, the same assertion follows by taking the lowest power of \(t\).
178	
179	All the rings \(V_i\), together with \(W\), are pairwise incomparable. Indeed, distinct rank-one valuation rings are incomparable, and the only rank-one coarsening of \(W\) is \(V_0\), whose residue field is not finite.
180	
181	### 3.2 An intersection whose maximal localizations are exactly these rings
182	
183	Set
184	\[
185	E=W\cap\bigcap_{i\ge1}V_i.
186	\]
187	
188	We prove
189	\[
190	E\text{ is Prüfer, with maximal localizations exactly }W,V_1,V_2,\ldots. \tag{8}
191	\]
192	
193	For any \(x\in K\), the three elements
194	\[
195	\frac1{1+x^2},\qquad \frac{x}{1+x^2},\qquad
196	\frac{x^2}{1+x^2}
197	\]
198	belong to every ring in this intersection. The reason is that \(-1\) is not a square in any of their residue fields. The first and third sum to \(1\). In a localization \(E_N\) at a maximal ideal, one of these two is a unit; their quotients with the middle element show that either \(x\) or \(x^{-1}\) belongs to \(E_N\). Thus \(E_N\) is a valuation ring. This also shows \(\operatorname{Frac}(E)=K\).
199	
200	It remains to identify these localizations. In every valuation under consideration,
201	\[
202	v(x^2+y^2)=2\min\{v(x),v(y)\}. \tag{9}
203	\]
204	Suppose a maximal ideal \(N\) of \(E\) were contained in none of their centers. Choose an element of \(N\) that is a unit in \(W\). It is a unit in all sufficiently large \(V_i\), by (7). Choose finitely many further elements of \(N\) to cover the remaining \(V_i\).
205	
206	Repeatedly using \(x^2+y^2\), in a balanced binary tree, produces an element \(g\in N\) that is a unit in every one of the valuation rings. Then \(1/g\in E\), a contradiction.
207	
208	Consequently every maximal localization is one of the displayed rings. Conversely, incomparability shows that each displayed ring occurs. This proves (8).
209	
210	Write \(N_i\) for the maximal ideal associated with \(V_i\), and \(N_\infty\) for the one associated with \(W\). Let
211	\[
212	P=E\cap M_0.
213	\]
214	Then
215	\[
216	E_P=V_0,\qquad E/P=B. \tag{10}
217	\]
218	Indeed, \(P\) lies only under \(N_\infty\), and localization at \(N_\infty\) identifies it with the height-one prime \(M_0\) of \(W\).
219	
220	### 3.3 Collapsing the high-dimensional branch
221	
222	Define
223	\[
224	D_r=k+P\subset E.
225	\]
226	
227	The pullback spectrum description shows that its maximal ideals are
228	\[
229	P,\qquad M_i=N_i\cap D_r,
230	\]
231	and
232	\[
233	(D_r)_{M_i}=V_i,\qquad (D_r)_P=k+M_0\subset V_0. \tag{11}
234	\]
235	For clarity, localizing \(E\) at \(D_r\setminus P\) removes all \(N_i\) and leaves \(W\); its ideal \(P\) becomes \(M_0\). This gives the second equality in (11).
236	
237	Every ring in (11) has dimension \(1\). Hence
238	\[
239	\dim D_r=1.
240	\]
241	
242	Also \(\dim D_r[X]=3\). The upper bound is Seidenberg's inequality. For the lower bound, work in \(A=k+M_0\), and choose \(u\in L\) transcendental over \(k\). In \(A[X]\),
243	\[
244	0\subsetneq (X-u)K[X]\cap A[X]
245	 \subsetneq M_0[X]\subsetneq M_0[X]+(X)
246	\]
247	is a prime chain. The middle containment holds because reduction of a polynomial vanishing at \(u\) gives a polynomial over \(k\) vanishing at a transcendental element.
248	
249	### 3.4 Computing the localization of \(\operatorname{Int}(D_r)\) at \(P\)
250	
251	Let
252	\[
253	R=\{f\in W[X]: f(a)\in k+M_0\text{ for all }a\in k\}.
254	\]
255	We claim
256	\[
257	\operatorname{Int}(D_r)_{D_r\setminus P}=R. \tag{12}
258	\]
259	
260	First, if \(f\in\operatorname{Int}(D_r)\) has degree \(n\), then its coefficients belong to \(V_i\) whenever \(|k_i|>n\), by Vandermonde interpolation modulo \(M_i\). By (7), they belong to \(W\). Evaluation on \(k\) gives the other defining condition of \(R\). Elements of \(D_r\setminus P\) are units in \(W\), so this proves one inclusion in (12).
261	
262	Conversely, take \(f\in R\). Its coefficients fail to belong to \(V_i\) for only finitely many \(i\). By approximation for the distinct rank-one valuations \(V_0,V_i\), choose \(x\in K\) that has positive \(V_0\)-value and sufficiently negative value at these finitely many \(V_i\). Then
263	\[
264	s=\frac1{1+x^2}
265	\]
266	belongs to \(D_r\setminus P\), and \(sf\in V_i[X]\) for every \(i\). Also \(sf\) maps \(D_r\) into \(k+M_0=(D_r)_P\). Since
267	\[
268	D_r=(k+M_0)\cap\bigcap_iV_i,
269	\]
270	we have \(sf\in\operatorname{Int}(D_r)\). This proves (12).
271	
272	Put \(h=X^3-X\). Reduction modulo \(M_0[X]\) identifies
273	\[
274	R/M_0[X]=C:=k[X]+hB[X]. \tag{13}
275	\]
276	Indeed, division by \(h\) and interpolation at the three elements of \(k\) show that a polynomial over \(B\) maps \(k\) into \(k\) exactly when its remainder modulo \(h\) belongs to \(k[X]\).
277	
278	We now compute
279	\[
280	\dim C=r+1. \tag{14}
281	\]
282	
283	Let \(C_0=k+hB[X]\). A useful elementary fact is
284	\[
285	\dim(k+I)\le\dim T
286	\]
287	for an ideal \(I\) of a domain \(T\), when \(k\subset T\) is a field and \(k\cap I=0\). To see this, chains outside \(V(I)\) lift to \(T\). If such a chain ends below the maximal ideal \(I\) of \(k+I\), and \(Q\) is its last lifted prime, then \(Q+I\ne T\); a prime above \(Q+I\) completes a chain in \(T\).
288	
289	Applying this to \(T=B[X]\) gives \(\dim C_0\le r+1\). For the reverse inequality, take the rank-\(r\) prime chain of \(B\), extend it to \(B[X]\), and append the prime obtained by adjoining \(X^2+1\) over the maximal ideal of \(B\). All these primes avoid \(hB[X]\), and their contractions give a chain of length \(r+1\) in \(C_0\). Thus \(\dim C_0=r+1\).
290	
291	Finally, \(C=C_0[X]\) is integral over \(C_0\), because
292	\[
293	X^3-X-h=0
294	\]
295	is monic with coefficients in \(C_0\). This proves (14).
296	
297	Apply the conductor dimension lemma to
298	\[
299	R\subset W[X],\qquad I=M_0[X].
300	\]
301	A prime of \(W[X]\) not containing \(I\) contracts to zero in \(W\), so outside-\(V(I)\) chains have length at most \(1\). Moreover,
302	\[
303	R_I=W[X]_I
304	\]
305	because \(hW[X]\subset R\) and \(h\notin I\). This local ring is the rank-one Gauss valuation ring associated with \(V_0\). Therefore \(\operatorname{ht}_R I=1\), and
306	\[
307	\dim R=1+\dim C=r+2. \tag{15}
308	\]
309	
310	At each \(M_i\), the localization of \(\operatorname{Int}(D_r)\) contains \(V_i[X]\), so its dimension is at most \(2\), by the valuation bound for a DVR. Dimension can be computed by these localizations together with the localization at \(P\). Equations (12) and (15) consequently give
311	\[
312	\dim\operatorname{Int}(D_r)=r+2.
313	\]
314	This completes (6).
315	
316	## 4. Raising both dimensions by one
317	
318	Let \(D\) be any infinite domain, \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(D)\), and set
319	\[
320	D^+=D+zF[[z]].
321	\]
322	Then
323	\[
324	\begin{aligned}
325	\dim D^+[X]&=\dim D[X]+1,\\
326	\dim\operatorname{Int}(D^+)&=\dim\operatorname{Int}(D)+1.
327	\end{aligned} \tag{16}
328	\]
329	
330	Here are the details. Put \(V=F[[z]]\), \(I=zV[X]\). We have
331	\[
332	D^+[X]=D[X]+I
333	\]
334	and
335	\[
336	\operatorname{Int}(D^+)=\operatorname{Int}(D)+I. \tag{17}
337	\]
338	
339	To prove the second equality, an integer-valued polynomial on \(D^+\) must have coefficients in \(V\): otherwise its lowest \(z\)-order part would give a nonzero polynomial over \(F\) vanishing on the infinite set \(D\). Reduction modulo \(z\) must then be integer-valued on \(D\). The converse is immediate.
340	
341	More generally, for a subring \(B\subset F[X]\) with fraction field \(F(X)\), the inverse image \(A=B+I\) in \(V[X]\) has
342	\[
343	\dim A=1+\dim B.
344	\]
345	Indeed, \(A_I=V[X]_I\) has dimension \(1\), while primes outside \(V(I)\) form chains of length at most \(1\). Apply the conductor dimension lemma. Taking \(B=D[X]\) and \(B=\operatorname{Int}(D)\) proves (16).
346	
347	Now let \(a\ge3\) and \(b\ge a-1\). Set
348	\[
349	r=b-a+1\ge0.
350	\]
351	Start with \(D_r\), whose pair is \((3,r+2)\), and apply \(D\mapsto D^+\) exactly \(a-3\) times. The resulting pair is
352	\[
353	(3+a-3,\ r+2+a-3)=(a,b).
354	\]
355	
356	Finally, a field realizes \((1,1)\), and \(\mathbb Q[t]\) realizes \((2,2)\).
357	
358	## 5. Executed Python checks
359

The following Sage/Python checks the finite algebra underlying the construction: residue-field noncancellation, the complete remainder criterion over \(\mathbb F_{27}\), weighted-lex approximations, finite valuation jets, and the realization parameters.
